did_you_know.text: Shiloh served as Israel's early religious center — the Tent of Meeting was set up there before the religious center moved to Jerusalem.
At this stage seven tribes still had not received their final land allotments.
Joshua’s challenge—“how long will you be lax”—is an example of leadership pressing the people to take up their religious and civic responsibility.
The instruction to send three men from each tribe to survey and write up the land is an early example of an organized official survey or mapping.
The Levites receive no separate territorial inheritance: the priesthood was their inheritance, so they lived in towns within the tribes' territories and served the community.
Casting lots at Shiloh shows the use of lots to seek ‘God’s will’ — a common biblical method for deciding public matters.
Benjamin’s lot was set between Judah and Joseph — a central position located between different parts of the land.
The spring called Ein Rogel mentioned here is a historical spring identified near Jerusalem and appears in other ancient sources.
Calling Jerusalem ‘the Jebusite’ indicates the city was inhabited by the Jebusites before Israelite control.
